summary: Biodiversity crisis for ages 12–14: move learners from the qualitative claim 'lots of species are dying' to quantitative, evidence-based reasoning. They compare current extinction rates (~100–1000× the natural background rate, prompting discussion of a possible sixth mass extinction) against that background, examine how loss is estimated (species-area relationship, population viability analysis, IUCN Red List categories/criteria) as models with inputs, outputs and uncertainty, evaluate rewilding case studies as evidence (Yellowstone wolf trophic cascade; Iberian lynx recovery), apply minimum viable population and extinction debt, and debate conservation triage as a values question informed by — but not settled by — data.
misconceptions: 'Extinction is unnatural / never happened before humans' — extinction is normal; the crisis is the RATE, far above background, and the human cause.
'We can count exactly how many species are going extinct' — rates are ESTIMATES from models (species-area, PVA) with real uncertainty.
'If some individuals survive, the species will recover' — below the minimum viable population, extinction can be inevitable (extinction debt, inbreeding).
'Rewilding always works and the wolves single-handedly changed the rivers' — case outcomes are complex, contested, and multi-causal; evidence must be weighed.
'Science tells us which species to save' — triage is an ethical/values judgement informed by, but not determined by, data.

activities.title: Measure the crisis: species-area and population viability models
steps: Work with a species-area relationship: change the amount of habitat lost and read off the projected species loss, noting whether halving habitat halves species (it does not — the relationship is non-linear, so halving habitat loses well under half of species).

Work with a population viability model: set a population's size and variability over a chosen time span and observe how the extinction-probability curve rises as the population falls, with the minimum viable population threshold marked.

Identify a case where a population still has survivors above zero yet has a high projected risk of sliding toward extinction, and name why (for example extinction debt, or small-population effects such as inbreeding, loss of genetic diversity and chance events that raise extinction risk when numbers fall below the minimum viable population).
State in writing, for each model, what its inputs and outputs are and one assumption or source of uncertainty in the estimate.
activities.insight: The crisis is defined by a measurable RATE far above background and by models with real uncertainty, not by rhetoric; species loss does not track habitat loss linearly, and a population above zero can still face a high projected risk of extinction.

activities.title: Rate versus number: evaluating the 'extinction is natural' argument
steps: Read the claim 'Today's extinctions are just natural — there's no real crisis' and respond in writing using the idea of a background rate.
Explain the difference between the NUMBER of extinctions and the RATE of extinction, and state which one signals a crisis.

Plot the present-day extinction rate relative to the background rate and the 'big five' past mass-extinction episodes on a log-scale comparison, noting that today's elevated rate is discussed as a possible sixth mass extinction rather than a confirmed one, and name the human drivers (habitat loss, climate change, invasive species).
Name at least one method scientists use to estimate the rate against background (e.g. species-area relationship, IUCN Red List categories).
activities.insight: Extinction is a normal background process; the crisis is the accelerated RATE (~100–1000× background) driven by human activity — reasoning from rate relative to background, not from the mere occurrence of extinction, is the key move.

activities.title: Weighing a rewilding case: evidenced versus inferred
steps: Follow the Yellowstone wolf reintroduction as a cause-effect chain: wolves → changes in herbivore behaviour/numbers → vegetation recovery → effects on riverbanks and courses.

For each link in the chain, label whether it is directly measured/evidenced or inferred, and identify at least one confound (e.g. was a river change purely wolf-driven, or also affected by climate, drought, beaver populations or other factors?).
Compare with a second case (Iberian lynx recovery) and state what the data do and do not show.
Write a one-paragraph evidence-weighted judgement: how strong is the claim that reintroduction caused each outcome?
activities.insight: Rewilding outcomes are complex, multi-causal and contested; reintroduction can trigger far-reaching trophic cascades, but each causal link must be weighed against the evidence and possible confounds rather than accepted as a single-cause story.

activities.title: Conservation triage: defending a priority under a budget
steps: Take a limited conservation budget and choose which of several competing species to fund — for example a charismatic species, an ecological keystone species, and an evolutionarily unique species.
Use available data (cost, probability of success, ecological/uniqueness value, population viability) to inform the choice, and state projected outcomes for the allocation made.
In role-play or discussion with a challenger (e.g. a peer or teacher acting as a conservation biologist), defend the prioritisation and respond when pressed on the trade-offs.

Explicitly separate the empirical questions (what will happen to each population?) from the ethical one (which species should we prioritise?), and state where the decision rests on values rather than data.
activities.insight: Conservation triage is an ethical/values judgement informed by — but not determined by — data; finite resources force hard choices, and 'which species to save' has no purely scientific answer.

checkQuestion: Extinctions have happened throughout Earth's history. A student argues: 'Today's extinctions are just natural — there's no real crisis.' Using the idea of a background rate, explain whether they're right.
checkAnswer: They're wrong. Extinction is normal at a slow 'background rate', but today species are being lost roughly 100 to 1000 times faster than that background rate — and that accelerated rate, driven by human activity (habitat loss, climate change, invasive species), is what makes it a crisis, not the mere fact that extinctions happen. Scientists measure it against the background rate using tools like the species-area relationship and IUCN categories; it is the comparison of RATES, not the existence of extinction, that matters.
